content: Eosinophilic folliculitis (EF) is a dermatological condition characterized by an intensely itchy rash. The exact cause of this condition remains unknown. It is most commonly observed in individuals with HIV, particularly those with advanced disease and low T-helper cell counts. However, it can also occur in individuals without HIV, where it is referred to as Ofuji disease. EF presents as red, itchy papules (small raised bumps) that are centered around hair follicles. These lesions are typically distributed on the upper body, sparing the abdomen and legs. The term eosinophilic folliculitis reflects the predominant immune cells involved in the condition, namely eosinophils, and the inflammation of hair follicles. Epidemiologically, EF is seen in both men and women, as well as children with HIV, and it occurs worldwide. It can also affect individuals with hematologic malignancies such as leukemia and lymphoma. Additionally, a self-limited form of EF has been observed in otherwise healthy infants. In some cases, EF can develop in individuals without any underlying conditions, with a higher prevalence reported in Japan. The pathophysiology of EF is not fully understood. Various microorganisms have been implicated as potential triggers, including the mite Demodex, the yeast Pityrosporum, and certain bacteria. An autoimmune mechanism has also been proposed as a possible contributing factor. The diagnosis of EF is often suspected clinically, particularly in individuals with HIV who exhibit the characteristic symptoms. Laboratory findings of eosinophilia may support the diagnosis, but a definitive diagnosis requires a skin biopsy. Histopathological examination of the biopsy typically reveals lymphocytic and eosinophilic inflammation surrounding the hair follicles. The physical examination of EF reveals the presence of eosinophilic pustular folliculitis, which is characterized by pustules and papules centered around hair follicles. These findings are well-documented in dermatological atlases. Treatment of EF in individuals with HIV often begins with the initiation of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) to restore immune function. Direct treatment of EF focuses on reducing inflammation and alleviating pruritus (itching). Topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines are commonly used to relieve itching and decrease the size and number of lesions. Additional therapeutic options include antifungal agents such as itraconazole, the antibiotic metronidazole, and the anti-mite drug permethrin, all of which may provide symptomatic improvement. Other treatments that have shown efficacy include PUVA (psoralen and ultraviolet A therapy), topical tacrolimus, and isotretinoin.
